column5: strayed from the way of truth
column6: The commentary contrasts a way that reaches its destination with dalal as losing the way; at judgment Wisdom's speakers confess that they strayed from the way of truth and lacked righteousness's light.
The commentary says the lost person has gone where no one knows; Wisdom's speakers say they journeyed through trackless deserts and did not know the Lord's way.

column5: fool cannot find the way to the city
column6: The commentary explains dalal as someone going where no one knows where; Ecclesiastes says the fool does not know the way to the city, making loss a failure to reach a concrete destination.

column5: leaders wander in a pathless waste
column6: The commentary contrasts a guided road with directionless disappearance; Job says God makes the leaders of the people wander in a trackless waste.
The commentary's blinded people cannot see the path; Job pictures leaders groping in darkness without light and staggering like a drunk.
The commentary's sirat is a straight way with an arrival; Proverbs depicts the righteous path as light growing toward full day.

column5: way of the wicked is darkness
column6: The commentary distinguishes an arriving path from losing one's way; Proverbs says the wicked walk in darkness and do not know what makes them stumble.
The commentary contrasts the straight sirat with dalal; Proverbs depicts people leaving straight paths to walk in darkness.
The commentary contrasts a guided path with directionless loss; Proverbs describes those whose paths are crooked and ways devious.
The commentary says a path has an endpoint while dalal loses the destination; Proverbs warns that a way may seem right but its end is death.

column5: way of life and way of death
column6: The commentary sets an arriving path against a lost way; Jeremiah explicitly places before the people a way of life and a way of death.

column5: walk in God's way and live
column6: The commentary asks for guidance along the path of those favored; Deuteronomy links walking in God's ways with life and blessing.
The commentary contrasts a path that arrives with a lost way; Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses and urges Israel to choose life.

column5: they do not know the way of peace
column6: The commentary's dalal is loss of direction; Isaiah says the people do not know the way of peace and have made their paths crooked.
The commentary says a traveler may leave sight yet still be carried toward an arrival; Isaiah recalls God making a road through the sea for Israel's passage.
The commentary's path has direction and destination; Isaiah promises a new way in the wilderness and water in the desert, turning a trackless place into a route.

column5: prepare a way in the wilderness
column6: The commentary's sirat is a road that carries travelers toward an arrival; Isaiah calls for a way to be prepared in the wilderness for God's coming.

column5: Isaiah's road read as John's preparation
column6: The commentary treats the straight path as a route of divine guidance; Mark applies Isaiah's wilderness-road language to John preparing Jesus' arrival, giving the road a Christian messianic reading.

column5: path of life in God's presence
column6: The commentary says the sirat goes somewhere; the psalmist says God makes known the path of life, whose destination is joy in God's presence.

column5: word as lamp for the path
column6: The commentary's blind travelers cannot see the way; the psalm calls God's word a lamp to the feet and light to the path, supplying the light they lack.
The commentary contrasts the guided path with dalal; Hosea's closing line says the Lord's ways are straight, the righteous walk in them, and transgressors stumble.

column5: guarding the going out and coming in
column6: The commentary pictures a traveler who leaves sight but has a destination; the psalm's close asks God to guard the worshipper's going out and coming in continually.

column5: kept on the journey and brought back
column6: The commentary says a path may hide the traveler while still reaching its end; God promises Jacob presence wherever he goes and return to the land.
The commentary's road has a destination; the Song of the Sea says God leads the redeemed people toward the dwelling of his holiness.

column5: walking in darkness without knowing where
column6: The commentary uses dalal for one who goes where no one knows; Jesus warns that the one walking in darkness does not know where he is going.

column5: make straight paths so the lame may heal
column6: The commentary requests a straight road; Hebrews urges straight paths for the feet so the impaired limb may be healed rather than further dislocated.
The commentary says a traveler can disappear from the observer's sight while continuing along a route; on the Emmaus road, the disciples walk with Jesus but their eyes are kept from recognizing him.

column5: recognition and disappearance at the destination
column6: The commentary joins leaving sight with eventual arrival; at Emmaus the travelers recognize Jesus at the meal and he disappears from their sight, after the road has brought them to understanding.

column5: Philip directed onto a desert road
column6: The commentary describes a traveler on a route with a destination; an angel sends Philip onto the Jerusalem-to-Gaza road, where the encounter that follows leads to the eunuch's baptism.
The commentary says a road has direction and destination; Paul's vision of a Macedonian asking for help redirects his travel toward a new destination.
The commentary says Joseph's disappearance in the pit leads into a travelers' route; Genesis gives that route an Egyptian destination when Joseph is sold to Potiphar.
The commentary reads Joseph's pit and sale as a journey with an eventual destination; the psalm retells the story as God sending Joseph ahead of his family.
The commentary says Joseph's disappearance leads into the road of travelers; Stephen's retelling continues with God delivering Joseph and making him ruler in Egypt.

column5: God chooses not to remember forgiven sin
column6: The commentary says the Lord neither loses nor forgets; Jeremiah's new-covenant promise says God will forgive and remember sin no more, distinguishing deliberate pardon from loss of knowledge.

column5: Jeremiah's promise applied to the new covenant
column6: The commentary's claim that God does not lose or forget meets Hebrews' quotation of Jeremiah that God will remember sins no more; Hebrews frames that promise as the new covenant established through Jesus.
The commentary says God's knowledge does not lose what is entrusted to it; Isaiah intensifies the promise not to forget Zion by picturing her inscribed on God's hands.

column5: Moses asks to be blotted from the book
column6: The commentary says God keeps people from being lost in memory; Moses invokes God's book while offering himself for Israel, making inclusion in the divine record explicit.
The commentary says God neither loses nor forgets; God answers that the one who sins will be blotted from his book, adding accountability to the image of divine memory.

column5: written in the book and delivered
column6: The commentary says none are lost from God's knowledge; Daniel says those found written in the book will be delivered at the time of distress.
The commentary says the Lord does not lose or forget; Jesus tells the disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.
The commentary says God neither loses nor forgets; Paul says the Lord knows those who are his, marking divine recognition as secure.
The commentary gives a secondary sense of dalal as something vanishing from memory; Peter links short-sighted blindness with forgetting the cleansing from former sins.
The commentary says the fabricated objects disappear from their adherents; Paul says an idol is nothing in the world, recasting their failure as the absence of a true divine power.

column5: turn from idols to serve the living God
column6: The commentary says fabricated objects leave their worshippers; Paul describes converts turning from idols to serve the living and true God.
The commentary says the day gathers people and no one is absent; Jesus depicts all nations gathered before the Son of Man and separated for judgment.
The commentary says nothing can be absent from the Day of Judgment; Jesus says people will answer for every careless word on that day.
The commentary denies that anyone or anything is missing from judgment; Paul says God judges people's secrets through Jesus Christ.
